title: A US Fighter Jet Hit an Oil Tanker in the Gulf of Oman. All 24 Sailors on Board Were Indian.
excerpt: The Palau-flagged MT Marivex tried to run the American blockade four times before an F/A-18 from the USS Abraham Lincoln disabled it. Omani authorities rescued the entire Indian crew.
body:
The oil tanker MT Marivex had tried three times before. On its fourth attempt to breach the American naval blockade of Iranian ports on June 8, the Palau-flagged vessel turned off its tracking systems, slipped into Omani territorial waters, and made a run for Iran.

An F/A-18 Super Hornet from the USS Abraham Lincoln ended the attempt with a single precision munition fired into the tanker's engineering and steering spaces. "Marivex is no longer sailing to Iran," U.S. Central Command wrote on X.

On board were 24 Indian nationals — merchant sailors whose presence in the middle of a geopolitical flashpoint now requires an interministerial response from New Delhi.

## The Crew Is Safe. The Questions Are Not.

India's shipping ministry confirmed on Monday that a fire was reported aboard the MT Marivex at approximately 1:30 p.m. local time, south of the Strait of Hormuz. All 24 Indian seafarers were safely extracted by Omani authorities, and the Indian Embassy in Muscat thanked Oman's emergency services for the swift response.

"We are coordinating with the Ministry of External Affairs, our Indian missions abroad, the Indian Navy, and the Ministry of Defence to ensure their safety," said Opesh Kumar Sharma, a director in the federal port and shipping ministry.

Sharma initially identified the vessel as registered in Madagascar, though other official sources identified it as flying a Palau flag. The MT Marivex, it turned out, was sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control — a blacklisted ship with no insurance, no legitimate flag protection, and Indian citizens serving as its entire crew.

## A Pattern of Evasion

Indian government sources told ANI that the MT Marivex had made four separate attempts to evade the U.S. blockade. On three occasions, the vessel turned away after repeated warnings from the U.S. Navy. On the fourth, it used Omani territorial waters as cover and disabled its signal devices.

"This pattern makes it clear that its intention was not above board," the sources said, adding that the ship was in an unladen (empty) state when it was disabled — heading to Iran presumably to collect oil, not deliver it.

The Marivex is the seventh vessel disabled by the U.S. military since the blockade began on April 13. CENTCOM has intercepted 134 ships and allowed 42 to pass for humanitarian purposes. The blockade was imposed in retaliation for Iran's effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world's oil once flowed.

## The Indian Seafarer Problem

India supplies roughly 12% of the world's merchant sailors. Many serve on vessels flagged in countries with weak regulatory oversight — so-called flags of convenience that allow shipowners to sidestep labour protections, insurance mandates, and international sanctions compliance.

The MT Marivex incident highlights a growing risk: Indian seafarers are being employed on sanctioned or semi-legal vessels operating in conflict zones, with minimal protection and no diplomatic cover if things go wrong.

The Indian government has not publicly addressed how 24 Indian nationals ended up on an OFAC-sanctioned vessel, or whether India's Directorate General of Shipping had any prior visibility into their employment. Maritime labour advocates have long argued that India needs stricter pre-deployment checks when crews are contracted to serve on vessels operating in the Persian Gulf during the ongoing conflict.

## The Broader Standoff

The incident arrives at a fragile moment. Hours before the strike on the Marivex, Iran and Israel announced a halt to their latest exchange of fire — the most intense since the April ceasefire. Tehran warned it would resume hostilities if Israel continued its Lebanon operations.

Meanwhile, a U.S. Army Apache helicopter crashed near the Strait of Hormuz on the same day, with both crew members safely rescued. The cause remains under investigation, and President Trump told reporters the pilots were "fine."

The strait remains effectively closed to most commercial shipping. Insurance is either unavailable or prohibitively expensive for vessels attempting the crossing. Oil prices, already up more than 60% this year, remain near $95 a barrel.

For India — which sourced more than 40% of its crude and 90% of its LPG through the Hormuz route before the war — every escalation at the strait carries a domestic cost. The MT Marivex fire may have been a minor incident in the wider conflict. For 24 Indian families, and for a government scrambling to protect its citizens in a war zone it has no part in, it is anything but minor.
